dashboard.verdict.big: Five-tranche strength ladder + regime filter + desk cap — but do not buy a challenge. The walk-forward has been run, and it came back as noise.
dashboard.verdict.p1: Of everything tested it has the lowest drawdown (−$1,058 against −$7,295 for single entry), zero failed and zero zombie accounts across 72 rolling challenge starts, median ending balance $100,409. It is also still +0.03R on the sample it was chosen on, and +0.008R on the 504 BTC trades from 1 January 2021 to 7 January 2026 it never saw (WALKFORWARD.md). That is a well-built vehicle with no engine in it.
dashboard.verdict.p2: Why not: a $999 challenge buys one noisy binary outcome. Five years of holdout just said the entry logic has no measurable edge. At a 14% industry base rate, passing once barely updates whether you have an edge — plenty of edgeless traders pass.
dashboard.xref.h2: Cross-reference — things that don't add up
dashboard.xref.f1.h3: 1. "5x scale-in for a larger position" does the opposite
dashboard.xref.f1.p1: At the same $500 risk, a 5-tranche strength ladder holds 34% less quantity than a single entry (0.109 BTC vs 0.167 BTC; $8,524 vs $13,000 notional). Because the stop stays anchored at T1's structure, each later tranche sits further from the stop and therefore gets less size.
dashboard.xref.f1.p2: The ladder's benefit is conditionality, not size: losers fill 1.66 tranches, winners fill 4.26. You're small when wrong and large when right. If what you actually want is a bigger position, that comes from raising risk per trade, and the ruin math says don't.
dashboard.xref.f2.h3: 2. The income model assumed 4.3× the trade frequency
dashboard.xref.f2.p1: income_math.py ran at 30 trades/month. The strategy produces 10.1/month (78 trades in 7.7 months). Every encouraging number in the $5k/month analysis — the 4-months-to-target row, $614 at the real 9/mo frequency (was $1,862 at an assumed 30/mo)/account — assumed a frequency this strategy does not reach.
dashboard.xref.f2.p2: Corrected: at 10.1 trades/month and 0.5% risk, $6,250/month gross needs +1.24R per trade. Not credible at any skill level. Either the timeframe drops below 4h to raise frequency, or the income target needs more accounts than the scaling table implied.
dashboard.xref.f3.h3: 3. RESULTS.md was stale on every row
dashboard.xref.f3.p1: It was hand-written and drifted from the engine after every change. It is now generated by gen_results.py from the live engine on the frozen sample, and verify_claims.py re-derives the published statistics from journal.csv and fails if either drifts. The table below is that output.
dashboard.xref.f4.h3: 4. The skill still describes the rollover trap as a general hazard
dashboard.xref.f4.p1: bitfunded.md presents it as broadly dangerous. Measured: it needs both uncapped risk ≥4% per position and a policy that holds losers through the reset. Under desk sizing plus swing_safe it is dead twice over — by cap and by policy. Largest floating loss actually carried into a reset was $3,422 against the $4,000 line, at 4% naive risk.
dashboard.xref.f5.h3: 5. Reverse-after-TP3 was untested; the trigger moved to the stop-out
dashboard.xref.f5.p1:
On TP3 it fired 4 times in 8 months, because only ~8% of trades reach 3R. On the
    stop-out it fires 24 times in the 78-trade sample, which is a sample rather than
    an anecdote — but it is still one asset over one regime, and the holdout (1 January 2021 to 7 January 2026)
    says the whole configuration is inside noise.
dashboard.xref.f6.h3: 6. None of it was in the repo
dashboard.xref.f6.p1: All of it is in kunjancollective/troid, and troid's ledger runs daily from .github/workflows/shadow.yml: fresh bars, replay, journal, ledger, commit. The journal's logged_utc column is the timestamp nothing can backdate.
dashboard.xref.f7.h3: 7. Two known small defects, both flagged and unfixed
dashboard.xref.f7.p1: income_math.py's withdraw=False arm reports $0 by construction — it counts only withdrawals as income, so the "bank profits to grow the buffer" comparison can't be sized. And risk.py accepts --json only before the subcommand.
dashboard.variants.h2: Where each variant stands — corrected numbers
dashboard.variants.note:
Ladder direction is the
  single largest structural effect found: same signals, same stops, only the side the
  tranches sit on. Weakness at 5 tranches is the worst profit factor in the project
  (0.14); strength at 5 with the reverse on stop is the best drawdown (−$1,058).
dashboard.risk.h2: Risk model — verified, independent of strategy
dashboard.risk.p: The budget cap is not conservatism — it is the only thing that makes the account survivable. At +0.35R, a genuinely excellent system, naive sizing at 1% blows the account 68% of the time within a year, and at 2% it's 98%. Every one of those cells is 0.0% under the cap.
dashboard.change.li1: Walk-forward comes back >+0.10R out-of-sample with a stable parameter neighbourhood. This is the gate on everything else. Run 21 Sep 2026 on api.binance.us: the config was chosen on 2026; on the 504 BTC trades from 1 January 2021 to 7 January 2026 it never saw, +0.008R, 95% CI [−0.023R, +0.040R]. ETH, 498 trades: +0.008R. Not met.
dashboard.change.li2: Frequency reaches ~30 trades/month, which on this structure means dropping below the 4h timeframe. Without it the income target needs roughly four times the accounts the scaling model suggested.
dashboard.change.li3: Reverse moves to TP2 or stop-out so the exhaustion thesis gets a real sample instead of n=4. Done: reverse-on-stop is the config, 24 reverse trades in the sample. It did not change the verdict.
dashboard.change.li4: Bitfunded's scaling plan — 10% net for 4 consecutive months, 2 withdrawals — grows one account instead of buying four. Cheaper, less to manage, and four correlated accounts running one strategy aren't four independent bets anyway.
